Hoot. Hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo. I am the one who answers the call at dusk, and the one who watches the meadow from the pine.

Hoot. Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the owl. I live in the hollow of the old pine. I call at dusk and through the night. My mate answers with a long, low "hoo" that sounds like a wet leaf falling. I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick". I live in the hollow in the old pine. I hunt voles and mice and the occasional shrew. I am not a barn owl, nor a scops owl. I am the owl of the wood. I am the owl of the meadow. I am the owl of the stream. I am the owl of the lane.

I am an owl. A tawny owl. My kind is called ke-wa. I am a male. I am called Hoot. I live in a hollow in the old pine. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" I hunt voles and mice and small birds. I am old, but I am still strong. I am the only owl in the wood. I am the voice of the night.
I am a tawny owl, the same as my mate. We are the only owls in the wood. We are called tawny, but the light on the feathers is like the dusk. We are the only owls in the wood.
A tawny owl. I am a male. I am brown and streaked, with a pale face. I have a pale patch on my neck. I am not a barn owl. I am not a great horned owl. I am a tawny owl. I am Hoot.

A stream, a road, a barn, a lane with lights. The stream is cold and fast. The road is loud and full of lights. The barn is old and smells of hay. The lane is where the lights go on and off. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous. I stay in the trees.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my beak. It is cool and clean, and it helps me stay sharp. I also drink from the puddles after rain, and sometimes from the dew on the leaves. I do not drink from the well, but I have seen other owls do so. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. The water runs under the meadow, and I hear it at night. It's a soft, continuous sound, like a low murmur. Sometimes it's louder when the rain comes. I can tell the difference between the stream and the river, which is farther away. The stream is my home, and I hear it every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. I can hear it from my roost all night. It runs through the meadow and the wood, and it sings in the dark. I can tell when it's full or low, when it's fast or slow. The water is always there, and I always know where it is. I can hear the water even when I'm not looking. It's like the earth is breathing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it from my perch, the water lapping and the fish moving beneath. I've seen reflections of the moon in it, and once I caught a frog there. It's not far from my tree, just a short flight across the meadow. I don't go there often, but I know it's there.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and wildflowers. In spring, it is full of insects and the scent of new growth. In summer, it is warm and buzzing with life. In autumn, the grasses turn golden and the insects disappear. The meadow, the stream, the hedgerows. I fly low, skimming the ground, listening for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. I circle the pine, the old hollow, the barn. I watch the shadows of the lane, the lights of the village. I fly where the wind carries the scent of prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meadow, wide and flat, with a stream running through it. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the stream is where the water comes from. Beyond that, there is a road, and then more fields, and then the village. The village has lights and noise, and people who walk with dogs. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the trees are tall and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A wood, a stream, a lane. The lane is the road, and the stream is the one that runs through the meadow. The wood is the one behind the woodshed. I hunt in the meadow, the wood, and the lane. I do not know the names of the fields, but I know where the voles are, and where the mice are, and where the shrews are. I know where the owls are, and where the foxes are,

Grassy place. I do not know what that is. The meadow is grassy, and I hunt there. It is wide and soft, and the voles run in it. I sit on a stone and wait. The meadow is not where I roost. I roost in the hollow of the old pine. The meadow is where I go to hunt.

Voles. The brown ones, the short-tailed ones, the ones that run in the meadow and the ones that burrow in the field. I catch them in the dark, when they are most active. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common, and the most filling. I eat them in the hollow, one after another, until I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are the best meal. I eat them whole, head first, and swallow the bones. I do not like shrews—they are too sharp and make me cough.

Voles. I hunt in the long grass by the stream, and I hear them under the leaves. I call, and they run. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the smell.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. The big ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the bank. I hear them in the dark, the soft thump of their feet, the rustle of their tails. I strike from the pine, or from the fence, and catch them with my feet. They are the main food. I eat them whole, bones and all.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. The wood is old and rough, and the inside is soft with moss and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I call from there. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I have been here for years, and the ivy is as old as I am. The hollow is deep, and I can hear the stream from it. I have raised my owlets here, and they are gone now. I sit in the hollow and wait for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old pine, high in the branches. The wood is dry and tight, and the leaves fall off in the autumn. I have a small hole in the side, and a dry stream runs past the hollow. I can hear it all the time. The pine is near the stream, and the meadow is beyond it. I can see the meadow from the hollow.

I can hear the wind through the leaves, and sometimes the rain. I have a mate, and we have raised two broods. The hollow is safe, and I have no need to go far. The hollow is a hollow in the ash tree. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I have been here since the first frost. The ivy is soft and the bark is rough. I sit in the hollow and wait for the mice. I have a mate and two young. I call to her at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
